title: What is inside an atom?
new_ideas: a scale-in from a hand to a single atom that turns out to be an empty stadium (scale jump with a reveal)
the count of flashes kept as a live tally in the margin through the film
a cannon shell bouncing off tissue paper staged literally

lines.text: In 1909, in a darkened room in Manchester, a twenty-year-old student sat staring through a microscope at a tiny screen, waiting for flashes of *light*.

plan.see: A black room; one shaded lamp turned low; a young man bent over a brass microscope pointed at a small box.
plan.beats: +0.0 ink-on in near-darkness: the bench and microscope (1.6 s) | +1.8 the young man (Person, Edwardian shirt sleeves) | +3.2 push toward the eyepiece

lines.text: Each flash was a single particle, smaller than an atom, striking the *screen*.

plan.see: Through the eyepiece: a dim green field where tiny points flare and vanish one at a time.
plan.beats: +0.0 through: into the eyepiece circle | +0.8 sparks flare one at a time (slow, random)

lines.text: His job was to count them. And on that screen, he saw something that should have been *impossible*.

plan.see: A flash appears on the wrong side of the field — where nothing should reach.
plan.beats: +0.0 a tally grows in the margin as flashes come | +2.4 one flash on the far edge, brighter; a red ring circles it

lines.text: Some of the particles were bouncing straight *back*.

plan.see: Ride with a particle: it flies toward a thin gold sheet… and rebounds toward us.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris to a tiny gold sheet | +0.8 ride with a particle toward it (2 s) | +2.8 it rebounds straight back at the camera (snap)

lines.text: It was like throwing stones into a cloud of mist… and having one come flying back at *you*.

plan.see: A bank of mist on a hillside; a thrown stone vanishes into it, then flies back out toward us.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: mist bank | +1.0 a stone arcs in (trail) | +2.6 it flies back out (snap)

lines.text: That one surprise would tell us what an atom really looks like inside. So how do you see inside something nobody can *see*?

plan.see: A faint dotted circle on blank paper: an atom with nothing drawn inside.
plan.beats: +0.0 wipe: a dotted circle | +1.6 orbit slowly around it (5 s)

lines.text: Atoms are small beyond imagining. Millions of them, side by side, would fit across the width of a single *hair*.

plan.see: A human hair in cross-section, huge; along its width, a row of beads too fine to count.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the hair section | +1.4 pull back: the row of atoms becomes a hairline across it (3 s)

lines.text: No microscope can show you what is inside one. Light itself is far too coarse to make out the *details*.

plan.see: A wave of light, drawn like a wide ocean swell, rolls over a tiny atom without noticing it.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: the atom | +1.2 morph: a broad wave rolls over it (2 s)

lines.text: For most of history, atoms were just an idea: the smallest pieces of matter, solid little balls that could not be cut *apart*.

plan.see: Three polished balls on a table, like billiard balls, labelled in an old hand 'atoms'.
plan.beats: +0.0 stamp: three balls drop and click together · sfx click −22 | +1.6 note 'indivisible' in an old hand

lines.text: So how could anyone find out what was inside one, when nobody could ever *look*?

plan.see: Iris tight on one of the polished balls; its surface reflects nothing.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris to one ball | +1.6 hold on its blank surface

lines.text: The very word comes from ancient Greek: atomos, meaning *uncuttable*.

plan.see: The Greek word ἄτομος is lettered in ink on a scrap of papyrus.
plan.beats: +0.0 quill letters the word (1.6 s) | +2.0 note 'uncuttable'

lines.text: Two centuries ago, chemists like John Dalton used atoms to explain how substances combine — but they still pictured them as tiny, solid *spheres*.

plan.see: A page of Dalton-style circles with dots and crosses; they harden into wooden spheres.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the page of symbols | +1.6 morph: circles → wooden balls

lines.text: The answer to what is really inside came in four steps: a crack in the ball, a cloud of flashes, a bounce… and an empty *stadium*.

plan.see: Four small engraved icons in a row: a cracked ball, a spray of dots, a rebounding arrow, an empty stadium.
plan.beats: +0.0 assemble: the four icons (0.8 s each) | +3.6 ride along them

lines.text: Our first clue is a *crack*.

plan.see: Clue tag 1/4; title 'Clue I · A Crack in the Ball'.
plan.beats: +0.0 clue tag 1 | +0.2 title

lines.text: In 1897, in Cambridge, J. J. Thomson was studying the strange glowing rays inside glass tubes emptied of *air*.

plan.see: A Victorian laboratory; a long glass tube on a stand glows faint green; Thomson leans over it; his real portrait pinned.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: the lab (1.6 s) | +1.8 the tube glows on (bloom) | +3.0 Thomson (Person, moustache) | +4.4 ★P-03 cabinet card

lines.text: His glass tube was the ancestor of the old television screen. But what *were* the rays?

plan.see: The tube's outline ghosts into the shape of an old TV set, then back.
plan.beats: +0.0 the tube morphs into a TV outline and back (2 s)

lines.text: With magnets and charged plates, he bent the rays and weighed them. They were made of particles — and those particles were far lighter than any *atom*.

plan.see: Inside the tube, a thin green beam curves as a horseshoe magnet is brought near.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: the beam (trail) | +1.6 a magnet slides in; the beam bends (morph) | +3.6 note 'lighter than an atom'

lines.text: He had found the electron: a piece of an atom. So atoms were not solid balls after all. They had *parts*.

plan.see: One of the billiard-ball atoms cracks open; tiny dark specks spill from the crack.
plan.beats: +0.0 tear-in: a crack runs across the ball (1 s) · sfx crack −20 | +1.4 specks spill out

lines.text: Electrons carry a negative electric charge. But atoms as a whole are neutral. So somewhere inside, there had to be positive charge to *balance* them.

plan.see: A balance with minus signs on one pan, and a pan of question marks opposite; it sits level.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the balance | +1.6 minus signs drop on one pan | +3.2 the other pan fills with '?' and levels

lines.text: In 1904, Thomson proposed a picture: a soft ball of positive charge, with electrons dotted through it… like plums in a *pudding*.

plan.see: The question marks melt into a round Victorian Christmas pudding studded with dark plums; it becomes a diagram of an atom.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: a pudding on a plate (bounce) | +1.6 morph: the pudding → a pale sphere with dots (2 s) | +3.8 ★D-03 slides in

lines.text: Physicists liked it. It was tidy, it was sensible, and for a few years nothing contradicted it… *yet*.

plan.see: A textbook page shows the pudding diagram; pages turn, it appears again and again.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: a textbook | +1.4 page-turn ×3: the same diagram

lines.text: It made sense. The charge was spread out evenly, soft and thin, all the way *through*.

plan.see: The pudding atom glows evenly, calm.
plan.beats: +0.0 bloom: an even soft glow (1.4 s)

lines.text: And if it was right, anything fired at an atom would pass straight through, barely *disturbed*.

plan.see: Small arrows fly through the pudding atom and out the other side, almost straight.
plan.beats: +0.0 arrows fly through (trail ×5, 2 s) | +2.4 they exit with tiny wiggles

lines.text: Clue two: *flashes* in the dark.

plan.see: Clue tag 2/4; title 'Clue II · Flashes in the Dark'.
plan.beats: +0.0 clue tag 2 | +0.2 title

lines.text: In Manchester, Ernest Rutherford had a powerful tool: alpha particles — tiny, fast, heavy bullets shot out by radioactive *radium*.

plan.see: Rutherford's laboratory in Manchester: benches, pumps, glass; a small lead-shielded source spits faint sparks.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: the lab (1.4 s) | +1.6 Rutherford (Person, big moustache) | +3.0 the source spits sparks | +4.0 ★P-04

lines.text: Rutherford, a farmer's son from New Zealand, had already won a Nobel Prize for his work on *radioactivity*.

plan.see: A gold medal drops on the bench beside his portrait; a small map pin on New Zealand.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: the medal (bounce) | +1.4 a tiny NZ pin on a globe

lines.text: Alpha particles are thousands of times heavier than electrons. They fly out of radium fast enough to cross a room in a tiny fraction of a *second*.

plan.see: A single alpha particle drawn as a heavy glowing bead; ride with it as it streaks across the room.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris to the bead | +1.0 ride with it (2 s, linear)

lines.text: What would happen if you fired them at a thin sheet of metal? He gave the job to his assistant, Hans Geiger, and to the young student Ernest *Marsden*.

plan.see: Two figures at the bench: an older German assistant and the student from the opening shot.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: Geiger enters | +1.4 Marsden (match from L0) | +2.6 ★P-01 cabinet card

lines.text: They fired a narrow beam of alpha particles at a sheet of gold, beaten so thin that light could almost shine through *it*.

plan.see: A gold leaf held to a lamp glows green-gold through its thinness; a narrow beam aims at it.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: the beam (1.6 s) | +1.8 the gold leaf glows translucent | +3.0 ★P-06 real gold leaf plate

lines.text: The beam passed through a narrow slit inside a box pumped empty of air, so that nothing but the gold could get in its *way*.

plan.see: A cut-away drawing of the apparatus: source, slit, foil, screen and microscope inside an airless box.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: the section drawing (2 s) | +2.2 labels source / foil / screen | +3.4 ★D-05 in a loupe

lines.text: There were no electronic counters. The only way to detect each particle was a screen coated with zinc sulphide, which gave off a tiny flash when one *hit*.

plan.see: A window into the box: the screen glows with a single faint spark where a particle lands.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris into the box (1.2 s) | +1.6 a spark lands on the screen

lines.text: So they sat in the dark until their eyes adjusted, and counted the flashes one by one, through a *microscope*.

plan.see: The room dims to almost black; slowly the eye adjusts and the screen's flashes become visible.
plan.beats: +0.0 light-change: to near black (2 s) | +2.2 wipe: flashes slowly become visible

lines.text: It was exhausting work. A person could only count accurately for a short time before the eyes had to *rest*.

plan.see: Tally sheets fill with strokes; the counter rubs his eyes and swaps places.
plan.beats: +0.0 blinds: tally sheets fill (stagger) | +2.4 the two men swap at the eyepiece

lines.text: Geiger later turned that drudgery into a machine that counted particles by itself — the Geiger counter, still clicking in labs *today*.

plan.see: A period Geiger counter on the bench; its needle jumps with each click.
plan.beats: +0.0 stamp: the counter appears | +1.0 the needle jumps (tremble) · sfx clicks −24

lines.text: Most particles flew straight through the gold, just as the pudding *predicted*.

plan.see: Ride with a stream of particles: they pass through the foil almost undeflected.
plan.beats: +0.0 ride with the stream (3 s)

lines.text: A few were nudged a little to one side. That was expected *too*.

plan.see: A few paths bend slightly as they pass.
plan.beats: +0.0 a few trails bend a few degrees

lines.text: Clue three: the one that came *back*.

plan.see: Clue tag 3/4; title 'Clue III · The One That Came Back'.
plan.beats: +0.0 clue tag 3 | +0.2 title

lines.text: Rutherford asked Marsden to try something that seemed pointless: look for particles bouncing back toward the *source*.

plan.see: Rutherford points to the side of the box nearest the source; Marsden moves the microscope there.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: Rutherford leans in (pose point) | +1.6 the microscope swings round to the source side

lines.text: Nobody expected to see any. A thin pudding of charge could never throw back a heavy, fast *bullet*.

plan.see: A pudding sits in the path of a speeding bullet; the bullet goes straight through it.
plan.beats: +0.0 the bullet streaks through the pudding (trail, 0.8 s) | +1.4 the pudding wobbles; nothing more

lines.text: But some *did* come back.

plan.see: The eyepiece view: a bright flash on the source side.
plan.beats: +0.0 stamp: a flash on the 'impossible' side (snap) · sfx glass tick −18

lines.text: In 1909, Geiger and Marsden reported that about one in every eight thousand particles was thrown back from the *metal*.

plan.see: The real 1909 paper ★D-01 unrolls; the sentence with '1 in 8000' is underlined.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: ★D-01 (1.6 s) | +2.0 red underline under the sentence

lines.text: One in eight thousand sounds tiny. But for a pudding, it should have been *zero*.

plan.see: Eight thousand dots fill a field; one of them is red; beside it, a pudding with a large red zero.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: dots fill the field (2 s) | +2.4 one dot turns red | +3.6 figure '0' beside the pudding

lines.text: Rutherford had worked with alpha particles for years. He knew how heavy and fast they were. A whisper-thin film should never have turned one *around*.

plan.see: Rutherford at his desk, pen stopped mid-line, staring at the tally.
plan.beats: +0.0 Rutherford pose → think | +1.6 the pen stops (tremble)

lines.text: Years later, Rutherford described his shock. It was, he said, as if you fired a fifteen-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper… and it came back and hit *you*.

plan.see: A huge naval shell flies at a sheet of tissue paper on a frame — and bounces straight back toward us.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: the tissue on its frame | +1.4 the shell flies (ride 2 s) | +4.0 it rebounds at the camera (snap) | +5.0 plate with the quotation

lines.text: There was only one explanation. Inside the atom, there had to be something tiny, heavy, and fiercely *charged*.

plan.see: The pudding fades; at the centre of the atom outline, a pinpoint appears.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris to the atom outline | +1.4 the pudding dissolves | +2.4 a pinpoint at the centre

lines.text: Rutherford spent almost two years working out the mathematics of a single concentrated *charge*.

plan.see: Rutherford at a desk under a lamp; pages of equations unroll beside him.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: pages of sums (1.6 s) | +1.8 lamp flicker

lines.text: Most particles missed it entirely. But the rare one that came close was flung *aside* — or straight back.

plan.see: Particle paths fan around the pinpoint: most straight, a few bending sharply, one turning back.
plan.beats: +0.0 trails (×12) pass the centre; the closest swing hard; one reverses (true to ★X-01 angles)

lines.text: Then Geiger and Marsden counted again, angle by angle, and the flashes matched his formula *exactly*.

plan.see: Counted points rise on a graph and sit right on a drawn curve.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: the curve (1.6 s) | +2.0 points land on it one by one (true to ★X-01)

lines.text: Clue four: an empty *stadium*.

plan.see: Clue tag 4/4; title 'Clue IV · The Pea in the Stadium'.
plan.beats: +0.0 clue tag 4 | +0.2 title

lines.text: Even hydrogen, the simplest atom of all, is mostly emptiness: one electron, far from a nucleus made of a single *proton*.

plan.see: The simplest atom drawn: one dot at the centre, one faint electron far out.
plan.beats: +0.0 ink-on: centre dot and far electron (1.6 s)

lines.text: In 1911, Rutherford published his conclusion. Almost all of an atom's mass, and all its positive charge, are packed into a tiny centre: the *nucleus*.

plan.see: The real 1911 paper ★D-02; beside it, the pinpoint labelled 'nucleus'.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: ★D-02 | +1.8 red circle on 'central charge' | +3.2 label 'nucleus' with a leader line

lines.text: The electrons move around it, far out. And between them and the nucleus there is… *nothing*.

plan.see: Pull back: tiny electrons far out on the edge of a huge empty circle; the nucleus a dot at the centre.
plan.beats: +0.0 scale-out ×20 (3 s) | +1.6 wipe: faint electron haze at the rim | +3.0 the empty space between

lines.text: How empty? The nucleus is about a hundred thousand times smaller across than the atom *itself*.

plan.see: A gold ruler measures the atom; a tiny tick marks the nucleus.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: a ruler across the atom | +1.6 a tick at the centre | +2.6 note '×100,000'

lines.text: Picture an atom as big as a football stadium. The nucleus would be a pea on the centre *spot*.

plan.see: An empty stadium rises around the atom outline; the nucleus becomes a green pea on the centre spot.
plan.beats: +0.0 rise: the stadium stands (2 s) | +2.2 morph: nucleus → pea | +3.4 crane over the stadium | +4.6 ★P-08 plate

lines.text: The electrons would be specks of dust drifting around the highest seats. And everything in between would be *empty*.

plan.see: Ride along the top rows: tiny motes drift; the vast bowl between is empty.
plan.beats: +0.0 dust motes appear in the top rows | +1.0 ride around the rim (4 s)

lines.text: Every chemical reaction — every flame, every breath — happens out at the edges, among the electrons. The nucleus sits untouched at the *centre*.

plan.see: A tiny candle flame flickers at the stadium's rim among the dust motes; the pea sits still at the centre.
plan.beats: +0.0 bloom: a flame at the rim | +2.0 the pea stays dark and still

lines.text: Later, in 1932, James Chadwick found the other passenger in the nucleus — the neutron — completing the *picture*.

plan.see: A window: Chadwick at a bench; the pea-nucleus shows two kinds of tiny beads.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: a window opens (1.0 s) | +1.4 Chadwick (Person) | +2.8 the nucleus splits into two colours of beads | +3.6 ★D-04

lines.text: Now look at your own *hand*.

plan.see: A drawn hand fills the frame, palm up.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris: a hand (1.2 s)

lines.text: It is made of atoms, and every one of them is almost entirely empty space. So why does it feel so *solid*?

plan.see: Zoom into the skin of the palm: cells, then molecules, then one atom — the stadium again, nearly empty.
plan.beats: +0.0 scale-in ×1000 through the skin (4 s, geometric) | +3.0 the empty stadium-atom blooms

lines.text: Press it on a table. Why doesn't it sink straight *through*?

plan.see: The hand rests on a wooden table; for a moment it looks as if it could pass through.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the table | +1.6 the hand presses; tremble

lines.text: Because the electrons on the outside of your atoms push hard against the electrons of the table's *atoms*.

plan.see: Between palm and table, two clouds of electrons meet and push apart with curved field lines.
plan.beats: +0.0 push to the gap | +1.4 grow: two hazes meet; curved lines push apart (ripple)

lines.text: What you feel as touch is that push. In a sense, you have never truly touched *anything*.

plan.see: The tiny gap between hand and table glows faintly; it never closes.
plan.beats: +0.0 the gap glows | +1.6 hold

lines.text: Even the hardest diamond and the heaviest gold are mostly empty *space*.

plan.see: A cut diamond and a gold ingot side by side; through each, the faint pattern of mostly-empty atoms shows.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop both | +1.6 their atoms show through like lattices of dots

lines.text: You are solid, heavy and real — and yet you are built almost entirely of empty space, held together by electric *forces*.

plan.see: Pull back from the hand to a whole standing figure drawn only as a fine stipple of dots with wide gaps.
plan.beats: +0.0 scale-out to a full figure (3 s) | +1.6 the figure resolves into sparse stipple

lines.text: So — what is inside an *atom*?

plan.see: The dotted circle from the opening returns.
plan.beats: +0.0 scale-out | +1.0 bloom

lines.text: A tiny, heavy nucleus at the centre, a haze of electrons far out… and between them, almost *nothing*.

plan.see: The circle fills in: a pinpoint, a far haze, and an empty middle.
plan.beats: +0.0 assemble: the four step icons slide into the circle and become its parts (2 s)

lines.text: We know because two young men sat in the dark, counting flashes, and refused to ignore the few that came *back*.

plan.see: The dark room again: Geiger and Marsden at the microscope; one flash.
plan.beats: +0.0 match back to the dark room | +2.4 one flash

lines.text: Not by looking. By throwing things at it, counting what came back, and taking the strangest result *seriously*.

plan.see: The tally sheet of flashes; the last stroke is drawn in red.
plan.beats: +0.0 the tally sheet slides in | +1.4 a red stroke

lines.text: That discovery opened the door to nuclear power, to medical scans, to the physics of the *stars*.

plan.see: From the microscope, ride up past three small vignettes — a power plant, a hospital scanner, a star — into the night sky.
plan.beats: +0.0 rise: three vignettes (0.9 s each) | +2.6 ride up into the stars

lines.text: And it began with one student, one flash on the wrong side of a screen… and the courage to *believe* it.

plan.see: The eyepiece circle in the dark; one last flash; the brand end card follows.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris to the eyepiece | +1.6 one flash | +3.0 light-change to the end card
